paper_metadata.title: EEG characteristics predict subsequent epilepsy in children with their first unprovoked seizure

quips_assessment.risk_reasoning: The study provides a clear description of the target population, recruitment setting, and specific inclusion/exclusion criteria. The sample appears representative of pediatric patients presenting to a university hospital with a first unprovoked seizure.

items.label: Source of target population
items.prompt: The source population or population of interest is adequately described for key characteristics (LIST).
items.evidence_snippet: Eligible candidates were children between 1 month and 15 years old who presented with their first unprovoked non-febrile seizure.
items.reasoning: The age range and clinical presentation (first unprovoked non-febrile seizure) are clearly defined.

items.reasoning: Detailed exclusion criteria are provided, including the exclusion of symptomatic seizures and status epilepticus to ensure a clean prognostic cohort.

risk_of_bias_assessment.label: Study Attrition Summary
risk_of_bias_assessment.prompt: Loss to follow-up (from baseline sample to study population analyzed) is not associated with key characteristics (i.e., the study data adequately represent the sample) sufficient to limit potential bias to the observed relationship between PF and outcome.

quips_assessment.risk_reasoning: The prognostic factor (EEG) was measured using standardized protocols, interpreted by blinded experts, and required consensus, which significantly reduces measurement bias.

items.label: Definition of the PF
items.prompt: A clear definition or description of 'PF' is provided (e.g., including dose, level, duration of exposure, and clear specification of the method of measurement).
items.evidence_snippet: EEG PAs were classified based on the presence of spikes, sharp waves, or spike-wave complexes, whether focal or generalized, that were considered abnormal for age and state.
items.reasoning: The paper provides a clear definition of what constitutes a paroxysmal abnormality.

items.label: Valid and Reliable Measurement of PF
items.prompt: Method of PF measurement is adequately valid and reliable to limit misclassification bias (e.g., may include relevant outside sources of information on measurement properties, also characteristics, such as blind measurement and limited reliance on recall).
items.evidence_snippet: EEG studies were coded by number and read independently by two pediatric epileptologists or neurologists blinded to the identity of the patients. Agreement regarding the presence of a PA was required
items.reasoning: The use of two blinded independent readers and a consensus/third-opinion requirement ensures high reliability.

items.prompt: Continuous variables are reported or appropriate cut-points (i.e., not data-dependent) are used.
items.evidence_snippet: EEG PAs were classified based on the presence of spikes, sharp waves, or spike-wave complexes
items.reasoning: The PF is categorical by nature (presence/absence and localization), and standard clinical classifications were used.

items.label: Method and Setting of PF Measurement
items.prompt: The method and setting of measurement of PF is the same for all study participants.
items.evidence_snippet: Awake and sleep EEGs were performed on a 12- or 16-channel machine 7–20 days after a first unprovoked seizure. The duration of tracings was at least 20 min.
items.reasoning: A standardized protocol was applied to all participants within a specific timeframe.

items.evidence_snippet: A total of 96 children met all entry criteria and underwent EEGs.
items.reasoning: All participants included in the analysis had the PF (EEG) measured.
